messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marlene Kowalski is a sixty-five-year-old widowed military medic who spent the better part of four decades working in field medicine and emergency trauma care. She is a composed, practically minded woman who has seen more than her share of catastrophic injury, and she had long prided herself on her capacity to remain steady under pressure. That self-understanding was fundamentally disrupted eighteen months ago when, driving home from a late shift on a rain-slicked highway, a truck drifted across the centre line and struck her vehicle at speed. The impact spun her car into the median barrier; when she finally came to rest, the cab was filled with smoke, the windshield had collapsed inward, and her door would not open. She remembers the sound most vividly — a percussive, tearing crash that seemed to arrive before she had time to register the truck's headlights — and then the smell of something burning, and the particular quality of stillness that followed. She was extracted by first responders and sustained serious but survivable injuries. Physically, she has recovered. Psychologically, she has not.

In the months that followed, Marlene noticed that certain things in her ordinary environment had become unbearable. Seeing a car with a crushed quarter panel in a parking lot, or passing a vehicle of the same dark blue colour as the truck that hit her, could stop her mid-stride. Discomfort that she initially dismissed as nerves would rise sharply and without warning when these images registered. These triggers function as a direct pathway into a state of acute threat: her body shifts immediately to high alert, muscles tensing across her shoulders and jaw, her attention narrowing as though the danger were present and ongoing. Loud or unexpected sounds — a door slamming in the hospital corridor, a backfire in the parking lot — produce the same response, and on several occasions she has experienced full flashbacks in which the moment of impact replays with a sensory immediacy that makes the present moment temporarily inaccessible. She is not simply remembering the accident; she is, in those moments, inside it.

The quality of the memory itself compounds this. When Marlene attempts to recall what happened, she is flooded by emotion before any coherent narrative can form — a wave of overwhelm that forces her to stop. She knows what occurred, in the way one knows a fact, but she cannot find language adequate to the experience; when she has tried to describe it to her daughter, the words have failed her entirely. This fragmented, wordless quality means that the memory arrives not as a story with a beginning and end, but as sensation and image — and when it does, it carries the same charge as the external triggers, returning her body to that same state of readiness and alarm.

To manage the persistent tension and the intrusive material, Marlene has developed a set of strategies that have gradually restructured her daily life. She distracts herself heavily with work schedules, paperwork, and procedural tasks, and when distraction is insufficient she tries to suppress the thoughts directly — pushing them down through force of will, a technique that works briefly and then fails. In the evenings, alone in the house she shared with her late husband, she eats — not from hunger but from a need to quiet something inside her that will not settle. These strategies do not resolve the underlying state of threat; they sustain it. The suppression and distraction keep her vigilance elevated, so that her body remains primed and reactive, and the overeating, far from providing relief, leaves her feeling ashamed and physically uncomfortable — a state that lowers her threshold for encountering the very triggers she is trying to avoid. The cycle has tightened steadily: avoidance narrows her world, the strategies maintain her arousal, and the arousal makes the next trigger more potent.

Occupationally, the consequences have become impossible to ignore. Marlene has begun arriving at work via a longer route to avoid a particular intersection, and she has twice left a shift early after a flashback rendered her unable to focus on patient care — something that, for a woman who defined herself through professional competence, she finds deeply shameful. It was a supervising colleague who finally named what she was observing and urged Marlene to seek help. Marlene came to the intake session guarded but exhausted. What she fears most is that she has become permanently unreliable — to her patients, to her colleagues, to herself. What she hopes, though she expressed it only once and quietly, is that she might find a way to remember what happened without it happening again.
